question: Where are blood cells mainly made in a healthy adult body?
explanation: Bone marrow inside the main bones is the primary site for producing new blood cells in adults. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T5#BMP111_U5_T5_h1)

question: What is the name of the master stem cell that grows into all different types of blood cells?
explanation: All blood cells start from a foundational cell called the pluripotent hematopoietic stem cell. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T5#BMP111_U5_T5_h1)

question: Which of these blood cells develop directly from the lymphoid pathway?
explanation: The lymphoid pathway specifically produces T and B lymphocytes for the immune system. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T5#BMP111_U5_T5_h2)

question: Why does the body constantly adjust how many blood cells it makes?

options.A: To match changing demands for oxygen and immune defense
options.B: To stop stem cells from aging too quickly inside the marrow
options.C: To ensure that all cell types are maintained in equal numbers
options.D: To prevent the total volume of blood plasma from increasing

explanation: Blood cell production scales up or down based on everyday needs like oxygen levels or fighting infections. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T5#BMP111_U5_T5_h2)

question: Which organ releases the main hormone that triggers red blood cell production?
explanation: Special cells in the kidneys sense low oxygen and release erythropoietin to stimulate the bone marrow. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T5#BMP111_U5_T5_h3)

question: What happens to a patient's erythropoietin levels if they develop long-term kidney failure?

options.A: Levels will drop, leading to decreased red blood cell production
options.B: Levels will remain completely unchanged despite worsening anaemia
options.C: Levels will rise sharply to compensate for improved oxygenation
options.D: Levels will fluctuate rapidly depending on daily dietary intake

explanation: Damaged kidneys cannot make enough erythropoietin, which often leads to anaemia in chronic kidney disease. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T5#BMP111_U5_T5_h3)

question: What two main parts join together to form a complete haemoglobin molecule?
explanation: Haemoglobin is built by combining iron-containing heme rings with protein globin chains. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T5#BMP111_U5_T5_h4)

question: What essential mineral sits right in the middle of a heme ring to help carry oxygen?
explanation: Iron is the key mineral fitted into the middle of the ring structure so it can hold oxygen. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T5#BMP111_U5_T5_h4)

question: How many protein parts make up a standard adult haemoglobin molecule?
explanation: Adult haemoglobin is made of four protein subunits, including two alpha and two beta chains. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T5#BMP111_U5_T5_h5)

question: What does cooperative binding mean when talking about how haemoglobin works?

options.A: Haemoglobin works together with white blood cells to destroy invading pathogens in blood vessels
options.B: The binding of one oxygen molecule makes it easier for subsequent oxygen molecules to attach
options.C: Alpha and beta globin chains share iron atoms equally between their respective heme groups
options.D: Red blood cells cooperate with platelets to form quick clots during minor vascular injuries

explanation: When the first oxygen molecule attaches, it changes the shape of haemoglobin so the next ones can bind more easily. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T5#BMP111_U5_T5_h5)

question: What is the genetic cause behind sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: A complete absence of alpha-globin genes on chromosome 16
options.B: A single amino acid substitution in the beta-globin chain
options.C: A premature destruction of platelets by splenic macrophages
options.D: An excess of dietary iron accumulation in liver tissues

explanation: Sickle cell anaemia happens due to a tiny change in one amino acid within the beta-globin chain. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T5#BMP111_U5_T5_h6)

question: Why do patients with sickle cell disease get painful blockages in their tiny blood vessels?

options.A: Excessive iron deposits destroy the smooth muscle lining of major arteries
options.B: Abnormal red blood cells change shape and block small blood vessels
options.C: Low levels of erythropoietin cause sudden failure of bone marrow function
options.D: Rapid destruction of white blood cells triggers severe systemic inflammation

explanation: The altered cells form rigid shapes that get stuck in tiny blood vessels, causing pain and restricted blood flow. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T5#BMP111_U5_T5_h6)
